title: Data skills: graphs, tables and patterns

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Reading and drawing the data resources of Paper 2: population pyramids, maps with data, graphs, tables, trends, plotting, and choosing the right graph for data given.

blocks.heading: Population pyramids
blocks.text: A population pyramid shows the age groups of a population as bars either side of a central axis, males left, females right, youngest at the bottom. The broad features are read by group. The width of the base shows the child share: wide, a high birth rate. The taper of the top shows survival into old age: a tall thin top, a long-lived population. The bulges and narrow waists show the cohorts history left: a waist at the young adult ages records a birth dip decades ago. Male and female bars are compared side by side, and a cohort's share is males plus females, both bars together.

blocks.heading: Significant features and patterns
blocks.text: A resource question starts with what matters: the river and its valley, the steepest slope, the main route, the settlement's site, the highest value on the table, the turning point of the graph. Significant features are the ones that explain the rest. A relationship is deduced by matching two patterns: where the settlements sit on the valley floors, and where the roads bend round the spurs; the pattern of one is laid against the pattern of the other and the link stated as a finding, not a guess.

blocks.heading: Extracting and describing data
blocks.text: Extraction means finding what the question asks for, the value, the place, the year, and giving exactly that, with its unit: the 2010 figure, the highest region, the wettest month. A description of data states the overall pattern first, then the main change and any exception, then supports each with figures read from the resource, units attached. Describing a graph year by year is not describing its trend: the overall rise, fall or stability is the answer, and the yearly values are evidence for it. A trend answer without figures is a shape without scale; figures without the overall statement are a list.

blocks.heading: Plotting
blocks.text: Plotting is accuracy: read the value along its own axis, follow the guide line to the crossing point, and mark it precisely, with a sharp pencil and a cross that does not straddle two squares. A value plotted against the wrong scale lands whole intervals from its place, and a point read on the wrong axis of a triangular graph puts a whole category in the wrong corner. On a triangular graph each axis is read along the angle of its grid lines, and the three readings for one point add up to 100 per cent, which is the check that the point was plotted right.

blocks.heading: Choosing a graph
blocks.text: The data decides the graph. Change over time: a line graph. Comparing categories, regions, months: a bar chart. Shares of a total: a divided bar or a pie chart. A relationship between two measures, one against the other: a scatter graph. A distribution over space: a choropleth or dot map. Three shares that total 100 per cent, employment structure for instance: a triangular graph. Movement between places: a flow diagram. The choice is part of the answer, and a graph that distorts the data, a pie chart for a time series, for example, loses the mark even when accurately drawn.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The pyramids here are the population structure of topic 1.3, the data is the themes of every Paper 1 topic, and the arithmetic below turns raw figures into means, ranges and percentages that the graph then shows.

blocks.heading: Pyramids, worked
blocks.text: A pyramid worked from its numbers. A table gives, as percentages of the whole population: 0-14, male 18, female 17; 15-64, male 30, female 31; 65 and over, male 1, female 3. The broad groups: children total 18 + 17 = 35 per cent, the working band 30 + 31 = 61 per cent, the elderly 1 + 3 = 4 per cent, so the structure is a wide base and a thin top, a young population pointed at growth. The sexes are close in the young groups and the women outnumber the men among the elderly, 3 against 1, which longer female survival produces. Reading a pyramid is adding the two bars of each group and comparing the groups, and Paper 2 asks for exactly that comparison in two or three marks.

blocks.heading: Significant features, worked
blocks.text: Significant features, worked on a small extract: a river valley with a nucleated village at the one bridge, a main road that bends round the valley's steep side, and a reservoir above the village on the high ground. The significant features are the ones that explain the rest: the bridge, because the village sits on it; the steep side, because the road avoids it; the reservoir, because the village's water comes from it. Choosing significant features is the skill, and the choice is defended by what each feature explains. Paper 2 asks for the features of a landscape in a short part, and the answer names the few that carry the pattern rather than a list of everything the square holds.

blocks.heading: Patterns and relationships, worked
blocks.text: Deducing a relationship, worked. A choropleth map shades a region's provinces by income, darkest on the coast, lightest inland; a second map marks the provinces' ports. Laid together, the dark provinces each hold a port and the light ones hold none, so the relationship is that income follows the ports, and the mechanism is trade: a port brings work, work brings income, and the shading traces it. The answer states the two patterns, then the link, then the mechanism, in that order, and every part of it comes from the two resources. Paper 2 marks the deduction, the stated link between two named patterns, and not the guesswork a learner might substitute for it.

blocks.heading: Extraction, worked
blocks.text: Extraction, worked. A table gives the monthly visitors to a park: January 2400, February 1900, March 2800, April 3600. Asked for the busiest month, the answer is April, 3600 visitors, and nothing else. Asked for the increase from March to April, the answer is 3600 - 2800 = 800 visitors. Asked for the month with the smallest total, February at 1900. Extraction is finding the cell the question names and giving its value with its unit, and it is worth its mark exactly when the right figure and unit appear, which is why the habit is worth building early.

blocks.heading: Trends, worked
blocks.text: A trend, worked. The visitors table above, read as a trend: totals rise through the period, from 2400 in January to 3600 in April, with a dip in February to 1900 that breaks the climb. The answer states the overall direction first, the rise; sizes it with figures, 2400 to 3600; then names the exception, February, and does not hide it, because the exception is real and the reader needs to know it is there. Describing the graph month by month, 2400, then 1900, then 2800, then 3600, is not a trend answer, it is the table read aloud, and the marks go to the overall statement the figures support.

blocks.heading: The trend told wrong
blocks.text: The recorded error is describing a graph value by value instead of the overall trend, or quoting figures with no description attached. The correct move: an overall statement first, the main change and any exception next, each supported by figures read from the graph with their units. The test: is there an overall statement before the detail, and do the figures serve it rather than replace it?

blocks.heading: Plotting, worked
blocks.text: Plotting, worked on a line graph whose vertical axis runs 0 to 4000, marked every 500, with the months across the bottom. The April value, 3600, is plotted by finding the April column, following it up to the 3500 grid line, and marking the point 100 units higher, two small squares if each small square is 50. The check is to read the point back: from the mark, come down to the axis and confirm 3600, and across to April. A learner who plots 3600 on the 3500 line has dropped one small square, and the read-back catches it before the answer is written. On a triangular graph the same discipline reads each axis along the angle of its own grid lines, and the three readings must total 100 per cent, which is the built-in check.

blocks.heading: Choosing a graph, worked
blocks.text: Choosing a graph, worked on three datasets. Monthly rainfall at one station, twelve values in time order: a bar chart or a line graph, because time-ordered categories are shown by bars or a line. A country's employment in three sectors, shares of a total: a pie chart or a divided bar, because shares of a whole need parts of one figure. The distances travelled and the fares paid by forty shoppers, two measures against each other: a scatter graph, because the relationship between two measures is a cloud of points. The data decides, and the wrong graph, a pie chart for a time series, say, loses the mark even when drawn neatly, because it hides the very pattern the data holds.

blocks.heading: A second table, read three ways
blocks.text:
A second worked resource, a climate table for a southern-hemisphere station.

| month | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| temperature / °C | 24 | 23 | 21 | 17 | 13 | 10 | 9 | 11 | 15 | 19 | 22 | 24 |
| rainfall / mm | 120 | 110 | 80 | 40 | 15 | 5 | 4 | 6 | 20 | 55 | 90 | 130 |

Extraction: the wettest month is December at 130 millimetres, the driest July at 4, the warmest January and December at 24 degrees. Trend: temperature runs a southern-hemisphere year, warm at the year's ends and cool in the middle, from 24 degrees in January down to 9 in July and back; rainfall follows the same swing, wet summers and dry winters, 130 millimetres in December against 4 in July. Relationship: the two patterns move together, the wet months being the warm months, so the rain is a summer rain, which is the geography the table holds. Plotting: on a climate graph the temperature is a line and the rainfall is bars, and the whole year is one page.

blocks.heading: A dispersion graph, worked
blocks.text: A dispersion graph, worked. Ten farms' maize yields, in tonnes per hectare, are plotted as dots against one vertical scale: 1.2, 1.8, 2.0, 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 2.4, 2.6, 3.4 and 4.1. The graph shows the spread itself: the dots cluster between 2.0 and 2.6, so the typical yield sits there, one dot low at 1.2 and one high at 4.1, and those two outliers are farms with something different, irrigation perhaps, or poor soil. A dispersion graph is chosen when the individual values matter, because every dot stays visible, whereas a mean of 2.43 tonnes per hectare would hide the two unusual farms entirely. The range, 4.1 - 1.2 = 2.9 tonnes per hectare, is read straight off the graph, and the cluster shows where the ordinary farm sits.

blocks.heading: How Paper 2 sets the data
blocks.text: How the paper sets the data skills. The same Paper 2 that begins on the map gives its remaining two thirds to graphs, tables, photographs and diagrams set in the contexts of the three themes, and every part is answered from the resource printed on the paper. The skills asked for are the ones this unit has worked: extract the value, describe the trend, compare the groups, plot the point, choose the graph. A typical sequence runs from a one-mark reading to a three-mark description to a suggestion that applies understanding to the pattern found, and the marks climb as the thinking does. The preparation is the same as for the map: worked tables, drawn graphs, stated trends, because the resource changes and the reading does not.
